articles.body: LeBron James, the four time NBA champion, has raised millions for his charity, the LeBron James Family Foundation, which directly benefits his hometown in Ohio. While he remains busy with his career in the league, LeBron James’ custom designed Mercedes Maybach does not seem to have made the money as many had hoped.LeBron James’ custom made Mercedes Maybach does not make the money it had intended to even after being constantly promotedAs per reports, a bespoke Mercedes Maybach S 680 designed by LeBron James sold for $390,000 at a Gooding Christie's auction during Rétromobile New York on November 20, 2026, below its pre-sale estimate of $425,000 to $550,000.This has raised eyebrows considering both LeBron James and Mercedes Maybach had been regularly promoting the collaboration for the last couple of months.Even just a few days ago, Mercedes Maybach made a post in collaboration with LeBron James which read as, “Every legend was once a kid with a dream. @kingjames has designed a unique Mercedes-Maybach with a greater purpose.”The post added, “Now, this extraordinary car is going up for auction to support the @ljfamfoundation, helping children pursue their dreams and become the legends of tomorrow.⁣ ⁣ On auction this Friday, November 20th with @goodingandcompany at @retromobile_nyc.”The luxurious Mercedes Maybach was crafted via the MANUFAKTUR Made to Measure program, with one vehicle kept by LeBron James and a near identical twin auctioned. It finished in a MANUFAKTUR-exclusive Light Ivory paint with matching solid-dish wheels and front-fender "LBJ" brandingA few months ago, in an interview, the former Los Angeles Lakers’ icon LeBron James had reflected on it as he said, “The chance to design my own customized Mercedes-Maybach was something I never even dreamed of as a young kid growing up in Akron.”The star player added, “To now have the opportunity to uplift my community and the families we serve through this auction means everything to my Foundation as we continue to build an ecosystem of supports that allows them to live out their dreams as well.”The proceeds from the sale of the Mercedes Maybach benefit the LeBron James Family Foundation's I PROMISE program in James's hometown of Akron, Ohio, supporting students and families with education, housing, healthcare, job training, and financial literacy.However, with the luxurious car selling below the estimated price, LeBron james has remained silent about it.LeBron James remains focused on his careerFor now, the focus remains on his impressive performance in the league.In his 24th NBA season with the Philadelphia 76ers, LeBron James has averaged 16.6 points, 6.7 rebounds, and 6.5 assists across 14 games (33.4 minutes per game), shooting 47.5% from the field and 27.5% from three.He has hit his stride recently with three straight 20-point outings, including a season-high 23 points in a 128–111 loss to the Portland Trail Blazers on November 24, 2026.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Lakers Trade Deadline Targets + Who LA Can Realistically Afford
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Lakers (15-3) share the NBA's best overall record with the San Antonio Spurs, and top basketball executive Rob Pelinka hopes to improve his team's roster ahead of the Feb. 11 trade deadline.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Lakers (15-3) share the NBA's best overall record with the San Antonio Spurs, and top basketball executive Rob Pelinka hopes to improve his team's roster ahead of the Feb. 11 trade deadline.

Pelinka said on the Spectrum SportsNet broadcast Friday: "We'll be active at the trade deadline to shore up things that we see. We think this team has a real chance to make a run, so we want to give the group as much talent as we can."

In practical terms, what might that mean for the team? What are the needs and available tools to improve?

Despite sharing the best record in basketball, the Lakers have several apparent flaws. As the 5 Things Still Hurting the No. 1 Seed Los Angeles Lakers recently mapped out, backup center is at the top of the list.

The bench tends to give up large leads, defensive rebounding is too sparse, and turnovers are too high. As the following slides show, the Lakers have financial constraints and limited trade assets, so they would need to replace the skill sets of any players they send out in a deal.

Landing a high-level, playoff-tested offensive threat like Naz Reid from the Charlotte Hornets may be too much of a " dream " for L.A. The Lakers should calibrate their sights to what they have to offer.

Some names to consider, in no particular order:

That's not a complete list of possibilities; how available any of those names will be by Feb. 11 remains to be seen.

The Lakers have only three prospects to offer if a win-now opportunity arises.

Cameron Carr, taken as the No. 24 overall pick in June, set a career high on Monday, scoring nine points in 10 minutes against the Utah Jazz. The 6'5" rookie missed much of training camp and the start of the regular season with an oblique strain. Head coach JJ Redick has been eager to give the 22-year-old guard minutes, but he's unlikely to play a major rotation role this season.

Adou Thiero, in his second season as the No. 36 pick in 2025, is a tremendous athlete who needs time on the court to properly develop. Redick indicated he hopes to get more minutes for Thiero to complement Austin Reaves once the team's starting shooting guard returns from a heel injury.

L.A. also has Bronny James, who hasn't cracked the regular rotation but remains a league-wide fan favorite.

Carr is earning $3.3 million in the first season of his four-year rookie-scale contract. Thiero is earning $2.2 million, with a team option for $2.5 million next year. James' $2.2 million is also followed by a $2.5 million team option.

The Lakers also have three players on two-way contracts who can be traded before the deadline if necessary: Chris Mañon, Arthur Kaluma, and Carson Cooper.

NBA trades are complex and often require extra players to match salaries or meet other technicalities, like roster-size limits or touching requirements in a multi-team deal. That's why players in the last year of their contracts can have elevated value, especially if the Lakers are taking in a player on a longer, more expensive contract.

The Lakers have quite a few, though some are vital parts of the current rotation. Their availability will depend on who the team brings back to replace them.

Jaden Hardy: $6 million, with a team option at the same price for 2027-28

Thybulle's defense and shooting are invaluable next to Dončić and Reaves. LaRavia and Williams have alternated as the fifth starter. The size of LaRavia's contract could prove to be necessary ballast in a trade.

Neither Hardy nor Looney is in the rotation, and both seem most likely to be offered by the Lakers to make the numbers work on a larger deal. Also, Thybulle, Looney, and Williams are all earning more than their salary cap figure, as minimum players on one-year contracts.

Free agents signed to standard contracts this offseason cannot be traded until Dec. 15. A Lakers move may not come until closer to the deadline.

Under the assumption that the Lakers won't move center Walker Kessler, Reaves, or Dončić, that leaves four rotation players on longer deals:

Quentin Grimes: $14 million; $60 million over four years with player option

Sandro Mamukelashvili: $13 million, $52 million over four, player option

Jarred Vanderbilt: $12.4 million, $25.7 million over two, player option

Collin Sexton: $9.4 million, $19.2 million over two, player option

While Vanderbilt and Sexton could be expiring contracts, those decisions are controlled by the player, not a prospective trade partner. Grimes is a valuable third guard who has filled in admirably with Reaves recently sidelined. He's unlikely to be moved.

Vanderbilt has struggled to earn minutes under Redick but has found a constructive role as an undersized center behind Kessler. Or perhaps Mamukelashvili is the center, and Vanderbilt the forward. The two-man unit has kept the Lakers afloat as much as possible, with Mamukelashvili an offensive connector who struggles on defense and Vanderbilt a defensive disruptor who struggles to score.

Mamukelashvili has slumped with his shot of late and is hitting just 31.3 percent from three-point range. Vanderbilt's contract is much shorter, but an acquiring team would plan for his $13.3 million on its books for 2027-28. Similarly, Sexton has struggled with his shot, at 27.9 percent from three, but has contributed important minutes off the bench.

When the Lakers made their big move in July, acquiring Kessler from the Utah Jazz via sign-and-trade, the franchise triggered a first-apron hard cap that limits its spending this season to $209 million.

With a full 15-man roster of standard contracts, the Lakers are currently $8.1 million below that threshold at $200.9 million. L.A. is nearly $470,000 above the luxury tax threshold and could try to slide under to save money—but that wouldn't match Pelinka's comments. Teams within reach of contending are the ones more likely to spend into the tax, and the Lakers consistently stay above that line.

As a franchise that went under the salary cap this season and used its room mid-level on Sexton, L.A. has no additional exceptions to work with beyond the vet minimum.

The Lakers would be able to bring back more salary than they send in trade, depending on the specific total. For example, Hardy, Vanderbilt, Carr, and Looney's contracts totaling $24.2 million can bring back up to $33.3 million—but that raises an apron issue. With the team's hard cap, it can only increase its total salary by up to $8.1 million, and that includes returning to the required 14 standard contracts. Teams can only go under 14 for up to two weeks at a time (28 days total).

The Lakers gave up much of their draft capital to acquire Dončić in 2025 and Kessler this July. Compared to most NBA teams, L.A. has meager assets to offer.

Still, the cupboard is not completely bare:

2027 first-rounder (1-4), though nearly useless given the team isn't likely to fall into the lottery

2028 first-round swap, the less favorable of what the Jazz swap with the Cleveland Cavaliers and the Lakers' own pick

2030 first-round swap, the less favorable of the Jazz and Lakers

2031 Washington Wizards second-round pick

It's not great, but it's what the team has to offer. The only other sweetener would be $8.5 million in cash.

Whether the Lakers make a blockbuster deal, a minor swap, or strike out entirely at the deadline, they can still explore the buyout market.

Each year, several quality players near the end of their contracts on lottery-bound teams are cut loose to explore other opportunities. They give their current team a discount on their remaining salary, opening a roster spot for a prospect willing to sign to a multi-year deal.

As long as the player is waived by March 1, they're playoff eligible. Whether they bring the kind of impact the Lakers seek is hard to say. Would the Jazz, once players like Jaren Jackson Jr., Lauri Markkanen, and Jusuf Nurkić return to health, buy out former Lakers center Jaxson Hayes?

Or would the team try to leverage him in trade to L.A. and, failing that, refuse to buy him out? The Jazz may also prefer to keep him, either as a rostered player through 2027-28 via their $6 million team option, or as a player they can trade next offseason.

Regardless, a one-year vet minimum contract signed on Feb. 11 would hit the team's cap at almost $845,000. A similar signing on March 3 dips to just over $563,000. These details may be pertinent, should the Lakers need to restore the roster to 14 after sending out multiple players in a larger trade.

articles.title: WNBA Trade Idea: Cameron Brink Joins Forces with Angel Reese
articles.summary: The 2026 Atlanta Dream came so close to winning a WNBA title. After an inspiring playoff run as the league's fourth seed, Angel Reese and Co. came up just short in Game 7 of the Finals against the Golden State Valkyries.
articles.body:
The 2026 Atlanta Dream came so close to winning a WNBA title. After an inspiring playoff run as the league's fourth seed, Angel Reese and Co. came up just short in Game 7 of the Finals against the Golden State Valkyries.

It was a grueling, defensive-minded series that ultimately catered to Golden State's preferred style of play, leaving the Dream in disbelief.

What does an organization do after failing to achieve its ultimate goal despite so much success along the way? Well, the easiest course of action would be to run things back. After all, Atlanta likely had more talent on paper than Golden State.

And in a seven-game series, one bounce here or there can make or break everything. It's easy to argue that Atlanta is already good enough to win the title as is.

But as any sports fan can tell you, life happens fast. Resting on your laurels is a dangerous game, especially when you don't have championship hardware to hang your hat on.

After coming within inches of WNBA glory, the Dream will likely be highly motivated to take the next step and find the final puzzle piece.

Atlanta is pretty set along the perimeter, but its frontcourt depth was shaky this past year with Brionna Jones nursing knee injuries.

What if the Dream could bring in a young, uniquely skilled center to pair with Reese? What if that player was also part of the same storied draft class as the reigning Defensive Player of the Year?

Atlanta Dream receive : Cameron Brink, Ariel Atkins.

Los Angeles Sparks receive: Naz Hillmon, Te-Hina Paopao, Atlanta's 2028 second-round pick with the right to swap with Chicago, and the right to swap 2029 first-round picks with Atlanta.

The Dream boast an impressive collection of talent at the 1-4 positions.

Jordin Canada, Allisha Gray, Rhyne Howard and Angel Reese are a fearsome quartet, and Atlanta doesn't have to worry about upgrading any of those spots.

However, there is a pretty large hole at center. That was evident in the WNBA Finals.

If Atlanta traded for Cameron Brink, they might be able to mend the flaws that Kiah Stokes and the Valkyries exposed.

For starters, Brink would give the Dream the legitimate rim-protecting five they've been desperate for.

For all of Reese's defensive brilliance, she is not a center. She excels at switching, hedging ball screens and making defensive plays in space, but she is not an elite vertical rim protector. Shot-blocking has never been a strength.

So why not bring in one of the WNBA's best rim protectors? When Brink can avoid fouling, she is a human eraser. Brink and Reese are a dream defensive tandem, a symbiotic machine that neutralizes each player's weaknesses.

Reese's versatility would ease Brink's defensive burden, while Brink's rim protection would free Reese from primary rim-protecting duties, allowing her defensive playmaking and rebounding to flourish.

Brink would also help the Dream's offense by opening up the floor for their guards and Reese to cook. Sure, the spacing Brink provides has been largely theoretical thus far, as she's shot just 48-154 (31.2%) from three in her career.

Reputation is everything, as Brink is still viewed as a stretch five. Maybe she gets to Atlanta and finally starts hitting threes in Karl Smesko's system, which wouldn't be surprising at all.

We haven't even mentioned Ariel Atkins, who also lands in Atlanta in this deal. She was very poor in Los Angeles last year. This component of the trade is a salary dump for them. Even so, the 30-year-old could bounce back in a bench role for the Dream, even if she is overpaid for the next two seasons.

Losing Paopao and especially Hillmon would hurt, but Brink and Atkins could easily exceed their production while elevating Atlanta's ceiling. Brink fits this core much better than Hillmon does.

The Dream is in win-now mode, so the 2029 swap they handed out here shouldn't concern them too much.

After watching Nneka Ogwumike suddenly retire and trading Kelsey Plum at the 2026 trade deadline, the Sparks find themselves firmly entrenched in a rebuild.

Their franchise player of the future is almost certainly not on the team yet. Los Angeles once hoped Cameron Brink would become that player, but that seems unlikely now.

The 2024 No. 2 overall pick hasn't had a smooth career so far. She struggled to stay on the floor in her first two seasons, tearing her ACL early as a rookie and playing just 34 total games from 2024-2025. The 2026 season was her healthiest yet, but she still missed 13 games battling ankle and rib injuries.

When she has been on the court, Brink has been a foul machine, limiting her defensive impact. Per Her Hoops Stats, she posted an 8.0 percent foul rate in 2026, second percentile in the WNBA. Apart from the fouling issues, she has been a solid, if underwhelming, player.

She's provided five-out spacing, some grab-and-go offense and elite rim protection/mobility on defense. Her turnovers are an issue, though, and she needs to start actually making threes.

All of that said, we're getting into Year 4. The time to coast on potential and pedigree is over. Los Angeles needs to decide how Brink fits into its plans and whether it wants to give her a large extension soon.

If a team like Atlanta comes calling with a deal like this, how do you say no? Though it might feel like you're selling a bit low on Brink, her injury history and lack of consistency could motivate the Sparks to cut bait for positive value.

Naz Hillmon, a starting-quality forward at age 26, is a good return to add to your collection of young role players. Te-Hina Paopao had a down sophomore season for the Dream, but she was solid as a rookie and profiles as a solid bench guard. Plus, Los Angeles adds to its asset stockpile with a 2029 swap that could be valuable if Atlanta falls apart.

The 2028 second-rounder Atlanta tosses in also comes with swap rights with Chicago. If the Sky struggle again, that pick could be early in the second round. You're also dumping Atkins' salary in this deal, opening up more cap space for free agency over the next couple of seasons.

The Sparks also have picks No. 6 and 7 in this year's draft. At those spots, Kentucky center Clara Strack could be available. She isn't nearly as good a prospect as Brink was, but she could play a dollar-store version of her role in Los Angeles.

All in all, there might not be a better time to move Brink and completely reset the franchise.

articles.title: 2023 NBA Re-Draft with Major Shakeups After Victor Wembanyama
articles.summary: Victor Wembanyama isn't going anywhere in our 2023 NBA re-draft, but a whole bunch of spots immediately after him are up for grabs.
articles.body:
Victor Wembanyama isn't going anywhere in our 2023 NBA re-draft, but a whole bunch of spots immediately after him are up for grabs.

The class that gave us the Thompson twins, a theoretically generational point guard prospect in Scoot Henderson and Michael Jordan's final, hand-picked selection as owner of the Charlotte Hornets is full of intrigue. Many lottery picks used the last three-plus seasons to deliver on or exceed expectations, while several more fell flat.

It's still early enough that many picks' career stories are still taking shape. We're going to make some necessary reordering decisions based on what's happened so far, but these are still largely early-20s prospects who could enjoy several more stages of growth.

As a reminder, we don't care about team fit or positional scarcity. This re-draft is all about organizing the 2023 class into the "correct" order—with the benefit of hindsight.

Victor Wembanyama's Original Draft Position: No. 1

It'd be nice to pretend there's any drama at this particular spot of the re-draft, but Wemby's status as a generational superstar and the dead giveaway in the hook make that impossible.

Already a unanimous Defensive Player of the Year and a great bet to win multiple MVPs before his career is through, Wembanyama is the rare no-questions-asked first pick to exceed expectations in reality.

The list of players to earn an All-NBA First-Team nod before age 23 is short. You'll be shocked to learn that nobody else in this class is on it.

Brandon Miller's Original Draft Position: No. 2

Miller makes it two straight re-draft slots that align with reality. His landing here was much less of a sure thing than Wemby's at No. 1, but a couple of factors make him the logical selection.

First, the market has spoken. Miller's five-year, $209 million rookie-scale extension is second only to Wembanyama's in the 2023 class.

Second, Miller's physical profile is basically the one every team covets. He may not become Jayson Tatum or Paul George, but Miller's size-and-skill combo invites those high-end comparisons.

Even if questions remain about the rangy wing's scoring efficiency inside the arc and foul-drawing prowess, Miller has put up three straight years of at least 20.0 points per game. He looks the part. His game has featured enough flashes of two-way excellence to make him a worthy runner-up to Wembanyama.

3. Portland Trail Blazers: Amen Thompson

Amen Thompson's Original Draft Position: No. 4

Plenty of people will clamor for Thompson to have gone ahead of Miller. An eventual switch between second and third isn't out of the question.

Clearly, this is a close call. Thompson got his own five-year extension worth exactly $1 million less than Miller's. If anything, he's proven himself more important to a winning operation early in his career.

While Thompson is an elite wing defender and A-plus athlete, questions about his offensive viability hurt his projections relative to Miller. Essentially hopeless as a three-point shooter (career 21.9 percent on 1.3 attempts per game), Thompson has limited off-ball value and hasn't developed enough craft as an individual scorer to justify putting the rock in his hands as a top option.

If that doesn't change, there might even be a case that Thompson should move down a handful of spots. A good team can only do so much in the playoffs with a non-shooting wing.

Keyonte George's Original Draft Position: No. 16

It says something that George's fourth season has been a little disappointing, with averages of 20.8 points, 7.1 assists and 4.0 rebounds. That's on him for setting the bar so high during a third-year breakout in 2025-26.

George isn't much of a defender, but he's quickly amassing data that suggests he's a first-option offensive weapon—one capable of shooting threes off the dribble, suckering defenders into fouls and setting up teammates. Wembanyama is the only 2023 pick with more total points. George is running away with the class lead in assists.

This is the best lead guard picked in 2023. It's not particularly close.

Ausar Thompson's Original Draft Position: No. 5

Ausar Thompson has been one of the most athletic and disruptive defensive wings in the league since his debut. This season's larger playmaking role is a welcome sight. Those qualities—stopping power and passing—are necessary to keep the 23-year-old near his original draft slot because the concerns about his shooting appear totally justified.

Can a wing who has made 38 of his 192 career three-point attempts (19.8 percent) ever play a major role on a championship contender?

The Detroit Pistons aim to find out, having committed $155 million to Thompson on a new extension.

There's no denying Thompson's No. 4 spot in VORP and No. 6 position in Win Shares among 2023 draftees, but questions about his viability as a postseason weapon will persist until he answers them.

Toumani Camara's Original Draft Position: No. 52

Detroit's love for Thompson made it too hard to take Camara ahead of him at No. 5. If emotion could be cut from the decision-making process, the guy originally taken 52nd might have been the right pick.

Camara doesn't have Thompson's stunning athleticism, but he shares his elite disruption skills and can similarly shut down opponents at several positions. A 2024-25 All-Defensive nod proves that.

Most importantly, Camara is now a high-volume threat from long range and may currently hold the crown as the league's preeminent three-and-D wing (non OG Anunoby Division). Camara drilled at least 37.0 percent of his treys in 2024-25 and 2025-26. He's hitting 38.0 percent this year on increased volume.

Cason Wallace's Original Draft Position: No. 10

A season-ending shoulder injury prevented Cason Wallace from proving he was ready for more on-ball responsibilities with the Oklahoma City Thunder, but the two-way wing had already shown enough in a more limited role to earn a five-year, $139 million extension.

Wallace secured that bag, the sixth-largest among his class, mainly on the strength of his wing defense. His 150 steals led the NBA in 2025-26 and helped him earn All-Defensive Second Team honors.

Though the 41.9 percent three-point shooting Wallace showcased as a rookie has yet to resurface, he's still hitting 37.3 percent of his treys in his career and may still have another set of playmaking and scoring skills he can access once he's healthy again.

Wallace is a great player to contrast against the Thompsons, as he lacks the overpowering athleticism and size of the twins but is so much easier to fit into a contender because of his low-usage game and reliable shooting.

8. Washington Wizards: Brandin Podziemski

Brandin Podziemski's Original Draft Position: No. 19

Third in the 2023 class in total minutes and assists, Brandin Podziemski is the final player we'll hit who played well enough to earn a nine-figure rookie-scale extension. His steady shooting (37.5 percent from three on 4.5 attempts per game), secondary facilitating, elite rebounding for a guard and penchant for taking charges all contributed to an advanced-stats profile that justified his hefty payday.

A role tweak is keeping him further out on the perimeter these days, but Podz rated in the 98th, 98th and 100th percentile in defensive rebound rate among guards during his first three seasons.

With a league-leading 38 charges taken as a rookie, Podziemski proved early that he could compensate for limited foot speed and athleticism with anticipation and a willingness to absorb punishment. He's the current 2026-27 leader in that stat and hasn't ranked worse than third in any year of his career.

Although he hasn't created enough separation to profile as a lead guard, Podziemski has established himself as a solid starter who contributes to winning in virtually every area.

Anthony Black's Original Draft Position: No. 6

It's all coming together for Anthony Black in his fourth season. On track to register career highs with 16.5 points, 5.6 assists, 4.9 rebounds and 1.8 steals on a 53.3 effective field-goal percentage, the lanky guard is going to make the Orlando Magic wish they'd extended his contract before the season.

Restricted free agency is no picnic, but Black is going to eat when he hits the market.

Shooting was always the concern for the original No. 6 pick out of Arkansas. Nobody really bought the 39.4 percent Black hit from deep on low volume as a rookie. He proceeded to validate that skepticism by hitting 31.8 percent and 33.3 percent of his triples in the following two years. Now draining over 40.0 percent from distance on real volume, it's time to acknowledge Black has arrived as a clear starting-caliber guard with star upside.

Jaime Jaquez Jr.'s Original Draft Position: No. 18

Even during the two-year stretch when his jumper abandoned him, Jaime Jaquez Jr. found ways to contribute with his bruising drives, clever passing and reliable two-point efficiency.

Now that it appears he can make threes again, it's even easier to see Jaquez settling into a starting role for the rest of the decade.

The No. 4 finisher in Rookie of the Year voting in 2023-24, Jaquez is also a two-time top-10 finisher in Sixth Man of the Year. He came in second last season as the Miami Heat's screen-free, fast-paced attack played to virtually all of his strengths. Now in a very different environment with the Milwaukee Bucks, Jaquez is proving he can adapt to any system. If his current scoring average (15.4 points) and efficiency (55.5 effective field-goal percentage) hold, he'll set career bests in both categories.

Don't forget the value of durability as we move out of "potential star" territory. Jaquez is third in games played among 2023 picks.

Scoot Henderson's Original Draft Position: No. 3

It's becoming clearer that it's not going to happen for Scoot Henderson—"it" being the uninterrupted rise to stardom many expected. Far from being the best point guard prospect since Chris Paul, Henderson is still only part of the way to proving he's a low-end starter.

Currently playing less (22.9 minutes) and scoring less (9.5 points per game) than in any season of his short career, Henderson is effectively an afterthought for the Portland Trail Blazers. The good news is that he still has much of the athletic burst, self-sufficient shot creation and defensive potential that tantalized draft evaluators. If he can harness those qualities, figure out how to be a legitimate three-point threat and take care of the basketball, there's still a chance for the 22-year-old to carve out a long career.

It's telling that the former No. 3 overall pick was probably closer to having his fourth-year option declined than he was to getting a substantial rookie-scale extension. Everyone else in the top five of the 2023 class signed for between $150 and $250 million.

12. Oklahoma City Thunder: Bilal Coulibaly

Bilal Coulibaly's Original Draft Position: No. 7

On-ball defense is Bilal Coulibaly's calling card, though true believers have spent the last few years tantalized by flashes of the rangy wing's potential as a shot-creator and all-around force.

A rookie hit rate of 34.6 percent from deep seemed promising, as Coulibaly averaged an intriguing 3.4 assists per game in a scaled-up facilitating role as a sophomore. Unfortunately, those were both outliers. Coulibaly hasn't shot better than 31.9 percent from three since his first season and is on pace to average one turnover for every assist in 2026-27.

Even with real defensive chops and elite disruptive skills—only Victor Wembanyama and the Thompsons join Coulibaly with at least 225 career steals and 160 blocks among 2023 selections—there simply may not be enough offensive juice for a long-term starting role.

As is the case with everyone else we're discussing, it's still early enough to hold out hope for more development. For now, Coulibaly is best used in a bench role.

Dereck Lively II's Original Draft Position: No. 12

Sixth in Rookie of the Year voting and a major contributor to a Dallas Mavericks team that reached the Finals in 2023-24, Dereck Lively II once appeared to be a franchise center.

If he could ever get over the injuries that have limited him to just seven games since the start of last season, he might look like one again.

Lively showcased great mobility for his size and elite rim-protection skills early in his career. Lateral quickness, anticipation, just enough of a nasty streak—all of the tools for a top-flight anchor in the middle were there. No skeptic could deny the 12.9 points, 12.2 rebounds and 1.6 blocks per 36 minutes Lively put up across 21 playoff games as a rookie.

Health trajectories that decline as steeply as Lively's don't often reverse, but the upside is more than enough to keep him in the mix—especially since he's still among the youngest players in the class. Lively won't turn 23 until February.

Jordan Walsh's Original Draft Position: No. 38

Originally picked 38th, Jordan Walsh easily makes it into the first round without much star upside. That's the stage we've reached in the re-draft, where the demonstrated ability to play rotation minutes on a good team is more than enough to make a climb.

Walsh broke out in 2025-26, starting 25 of the career-high 68 games he played for the Boston Celtics. His biggest contributions came on the defensive end, where the 6'6" wing posted a solid 2.0 percent steal rate and rebounded extremely well at his position.

The 50.9/38.4/77.2 shooting split he managed was an outlier not approached before or since, but Walsh continues to guard tough matchups and willingly fire from deep in Boston's system.

Noah Clowney's Original Draft Position: No. 21

One of six 2023 selections with at least 200 threes and 90 blocks in his career, Noah Clowney is easily the best stretch big to come off the re-draft board since Wemby. In fact, he's really the only other player in the class who brings any semblance of interior defense with his shooting.

Everyone other than Wembanyama and Clowney on that 200/90 list is a guard or wing who simply logged enough minutes to reach the block cutoff.

Clowney hasn't been an accurate gunner on balance. He shot 36.4 percent from distance as a rookie but hasn't been able to get above 33.3 percent in the higher-volume years since. After logging 60 starts in 2025-26, the 6'10" forward is now playing fewer minutes per game than he has since 2023-24. If his shot starts falling and/or he figures out how to pass the ball more effectively on his fake-and-go drives, Clowney could still secure a decent second contract in free agency this summer.

GG Jackson's Original Draft Position: No. 45

One of the youngest players in the 2023 draft was also one of its hottest starters. GG Jackson averaged 14.6 points in just 25.7 minutes per game as a rookie.

An athletic 6'9" forward, Jackson's high production was owed largely to a banged-up Memphis Grizzlies team that got only nine games from Ja Morant and struggled to just 24 victories on the season. Jackson took advantage of the green light, firing up 11.3 three-point attempts per 100 possessions and generally operating without many restraints.

A couple of less successful, similarly inefficient seasons followed. Jackson continued to showcase a scorer's mindset through the early part of 2026-27 but went down in November with a broken fifth metatarsal in his left foot.

Maybe he'll never put together a complete floor game, stay healthy or defend consistently, but Jackson still has the frame and bucket-getting instincts to move up from his original spot at No. 45.

17. Los Angeles Lakers: Brice Sensabaugh

Brice Sensabaugh's Original Draft Position: No. 28

Many will be surprised to learn that Brice Sensabaugh is the 2023 class's best sniper. Among picks who've attempted at least 500 threes in their careers, his 38.2 percent success rate tops the heap .

While you can question the actual value of Sensabaugh's counting stats, like the 14.9 points per game he averaged last year, the Utah Jazz's efforts to tank throughout his career doesn't diminish something like three-point accuracy. Sensabuagh is a legitimate bomber—on pace to blow away his previous career-best accuracy mark with a 44.2 percent clip so far this year.

Earlier this year, he logged his second career game with at least 40 points off the bench. At the very least, the gunslinging guard has established himself as a potent reserve scoring threat.

Jarace Walker's Original Draft Position: No. 8

It's tempting to drop original No. 8 pick Jarace Walker even further down the re-draft board, but the versatile forward showed too many glimpses of valuable rotation play over his four years with the Indiana Pacers to consider dumping him from the first round.

Though they were low-volume affairs, Walker canned over 40.0 percent of his threes during his first two seasons. Last year, the gap-year Pacers gave him 41 starts and the largest role of his career. Walker responded with respectable averages of 11.6 points, 5.1 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 25.7 minutes per game.

Still walking around in a frame that screams he should be a defensive weapon and still occasionally tantalizing as exactly the kind of capable two-way combo forward every team wants, Walker's appeal is still visible four years in. Not so visible that the Pacers offered him an extension, but at least visible enough to get them to pick up his fourth-year option.

Sidy Cissoko's Original Draft Position: No. 44

Recency bias is doing some lifting here, but Sidy Cissoko's work for the Portland Trail Blazers across the first six weeks of the 2026-27 season is good enough to offset the three less exciting years that came before.

In fairness, Cissoko displayed some defensive intensity and disruption in a little over 1,400 minutes last season. It's his growth on offense that has earned him several starts and easily the largest role of his career this year. Limited to this season, Cissoko's Value Over Replacement Player figure ranks among the top 10 in the 2023 class, ahead of guys like Anthony Black and Jaime Jaquez Jr.

Portland is short on forwards who can defend and space. Cissoko is doing both better than ever. At 38.3 percent on threes and a stellar 62.1 percent on mostly spoon-fed and transition two-pointers, the 22-year-old is contributing 8.1 points per game and defending ably on a winning team.

That's portable production worth rostering with a first-round pick, even if we're only seeing it for the first time this season.

20. Houston Rockets: Trayce Jackson-Davis

Trayce Jackson-Davis' Original Draft Position: No. 57

A lack of big-man depth allowed Trayce Jackson-Davis to see more early-career action than you'd expect from the No. 57 pick. Already 23 at the time of his debut, the second-generation NBA player may also have been a little more ready for the rigors of professional life than most members of the class.

TJD started a whopping 54 games and averaged just over 15.0 minutes per game across two years and change with the Golden State Warriors. Limited by a shooting range of "dunk" and not an intuitive back-line defender, Jackson-Davis never displayed a game fit for more than backup duties. He was solid in his role, though, and continues to play fairly regularly with the Toronto Raptors.

When TJD plays with high energy on the glass and has a guard capable of setting him up, he's a useful rotation big man. Through this season, he's eighth in total rebounds and sixth in blocks among 2023 picks.

Jordan Miller's Original Draft Position: No. 48

A popular breakout pick prior to the season, Jordan Miller suffered a torn left rotator cuff that required surgery in August. That derailed what could have been a career year and a climb much higher up the re-draft rankings.

We can still use the 2025-26 campaign that got so many fans excited to justify sliding Miller up from his original No. 48 draft position.

Though only in flashes, Miller teased Clippers fans with real shot-creation skills from the wing. He averaged 16.2 points, 4.9 rebounds and 3.7 assists on a 53.1/34.5/77.7 shooting split across 60 games, enough to earn a three-year, $15.3 million contract prior to his shoulder injury.

Already playing his age-27 season, Miller may not have much more growth in his profile. But the level he reached for the Clips last year is one most players in this draft still haven't touched.

Marcus Sasser's Original Draft Position: No. 25

He's only accessed it in spurts this season with the Dallas Mavericks, but Marcus Sasser's first three years with the Detroit Pistons were marked by some of the most reliable shooting in the class.

The Houston product entered the league at 23 with a clear understanding of his role. He's at 38.6 percent from beyond the arc and 85.8 percent from the foul line in his career.

Though Sasser has never matched the counting averages of his rookie year (8.3 points, 3.3 assists and 1.8 rebounds), he's been similarly effective in reduced playing time since then.

23. Portland Trail Blazers: Julian Strawther

Julian Strawther's Original Draft Position: No. 29

Just because he could never quite become the every-night rotation mainstay the Denver Nuggets so badly needed him to be doesn't mean Julian Strawther is some kind of bust.

Taken at No. 29 out of Gonzaga, the combo guard brought 6'6" size and some pretty solid per-minute scoring off the bench in three full seasons alongside Nikola Jokić.

Strawther has actually been on a quietly impressive trajectory, upping his points per 36 minutes (17.3) and true shooting percentage (59.0) to career highs last season. A knee injury is currently preventing him from building on those for a Denver team that needs his contributions more than ever, but his catch-and-shoot spacing and floater game will come in handy once he's healthy.

Taylor Hendricks' Original Draft Position: No. 9

Taylor Hendricks came into the league with an outside chance at reaching transformative-player status, a lanky 6'9" forward who, if you squinted, seemed to have the tools to be a multi-position defender, three-point spacer and rim-protector.

The ceiling was high. Unfortunately for the Jazz team that used the No. 9 pick on him (and for the Grizzlies team that took a flier on him as part of the return for Jaren Jackson Jr.), it's hard to imagine Hendricks reaching it.

A relatively inept decision-maker on offense, Hendricks mostly cleans up messes around the rim, finishes in transition and scores off setups. He's been decent enough at 35.8 percent from deep for his career, but he hasn't finished nearly well enough inside for a player with his length and athleticism.

A role player's career may still be ahead, especially if Hendricks continues to bring defensive effort. The days of expecting him to become a high-end starter on a winning team have probably passed.

Gradey Dick's Original Draft Position: No. 13

Availability matters, and Gradey Dick is one of a small group of 2023 picks with a health and production record good enough to earn at least 200 games of action.

Though he never delivered on his promise as one of the best shooters in the class, Dick has mostly been passable as a spacer while occasionally showing off some downhill driving and creation skills. It's easy to forget now, but prior to the 2025-26 season, Dick generated some hype around his facilitation game with a strong preseason showing.

Part of the package going to LA for Kawhi Leonard, Dick is reaching new levels of efficiency in a reduced role. On a career-low 3.8 long-range attempts per 36 minutes, Dick is knocking down a personal-best 48.0 percent. Specialist duties might seem disappointing, but we're nearing the point in the re-draft where a player seeing regular backup minutes is about as good as it's going to get.

Jaylen Clark's Original Draft Position: No. 53

If Jaylen Clark were a couple of inches taller, he'd have come off the board long before No. 53 in reality. Even after tearing his Achilles in March 2023, a player with his makeup and a little more size would have been worth a first-round pick.

As it is, the defensive-minded guard showed enough at his 6'5"-ish height to earn a significant bump here—pretty impressive considering he lost all of 2023-24 to recovery from that Achilles tear.

Clark is a rugged defender at both backcourt spots who can slide up to tackle wings in a pinch. His 6'9" wingspan and high-revving motor make opposing ball-handlers uncomfortable on the perimeter. Clark isn't afraid to gamble in the passing lanes when he's away from the ball.

Clark's true level as a shooter feels closer to this year's league-average clip than the 43.1 percent he shot from deep as a rookie and the 32.7 percent low he fell to last season. That's more than good enough to keep his defense on the floor.

Ben Sheppard's Original Draft Position: No. 26

A torn meniscus shelved Ben Sheppard after just one game in 2026-27, meaning his chance to prove he's a quality rotation piece alongside a healthy Tyrese Haliburton will have to wait.

Sheppard established himself in that role during Indy's Finals run in 2025, playing 21 postseason games, shooting 39.5 percent from three and defending with intensity. Like just about everyone else on the Pacers, Sheppard endured a forgotten 2025-26 campaign with Haliburton out.

It was encouraging that the 6'6" wing shot it better from the field and from deep last year, but he failed to build on the signs he showed during that playoff run. If and when he shares the floor with Haliburton again, perhaps Sheppard will recapture his peak form and convince the Pacers (or someone else) he's worth a guaranteed contract in 2027 free agency.

Mouhamed Gueye's Original Draft Position: No. 39

Who knows how much higher Mouhamed Gueye would have climbed if not for the fractured foot he suffered during a July 2026 workout? Prior to that, the athletic forward was a popular breakout pick who showed impressive defensive versatility and shot-blocking in 2025-26.

With enough lateral mobility to stick with guards and wings on the perimeter and the length to bother shots around the basket, Gueye turned in several impactful defensive stretches for a Hawks team that was often thin up front. All he needed to do to carve out an even larger role was prove he could consistently threaten opponents with his outside shot on the other end.

Maybe Gueye will take that step when he returns later this year. The mere possibility that he's a floor-stretching defensive ace is enough to make sure the 6'11" forward lands in the first round.

29. Indiana Pacers: Olivier-Maxence Prosper

Olivier-Maxence Prosper's Original Draft Position: No. 24

It didn't click for him in Dallas, but Olivier-Maxence Prosper fit better with the Grizzlies.

An unusual positional fit as a 6'7" power forward, Prosper brings defensive energy and transition speed off the bench. He's a good finisher ( 71.5 percent inside three feet for his career) who, this year, has been virtually impossible to keep off the offensive glass.

O-Max is deficient as a self-starter on offense, but he's learned to run the floor, cut and occasionally spot up beyond the arc. It's a small sample, but Prosper's two-way contributions this season, particularly as an event-creator on defense, help the Grizzlies to post a net rating 3.7 points per 100 possessions better when he's on the floor.

Still raw and still probably ticketed for a bench role on most teams, Prosper has a handful of skills that just barely keep him in the first round.

Cam Whitmore's Original Draft Position: No. 20

The Houston Rockets spoke, the Washington Wizards spoke and the Denver Nuggets are currently speaking. All of them have said, or are saying, that Cam Whitmore isn't the high-ceilinged steal he seemed to be when he came off the board at No. 20 three years ago.

An undeniable knack for scoring helped Whitmore rack up 12.3 points per game as a rookie. His role shrank the following year. The burly forward found himself on a second and third NBA team before his rookie-scale deal expired.

It's hard to believe Whitmore will ever live up to his potential. He has work to do to shake off the reputation that says he's not wired to play winning-team basketball. But all the undeniable positives that got him drafted—great size on the wing, the ability to generate his own shots, downhill aggression—are in there somewhere.

If only as a way of acknowledging that the tools are still too tantalizing to leave out of the first round entirely, we're giving Whitmore the 30th and final spot here. He may not have done enough to deserve it, but it's possible he'll finally put everything together at some point. That's more than can be said about anyone else left in the mix.

Stats courtesy of NBA.com , Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass . Salary info via Spotrac .

Grant Hughes covers the NBA for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, where he appears with Bleacher Report's Dan Favale .

articles.title: Geno Auriemma Rips UConn After South Carolina Loss, 'Having a Really Hard Time Coaching This Team'
articles.summary: UConn head women's basketball coach Geno Auriemma was left searching for answers Tuesday night after a 65-56 loss to South Carolina dropped the Huskies to 4-3 on the season.
articles.body:
UConn head women's basketball coach Geno Auriemma was left searching for answers Tuesday night after a 65-56 loss to South Carolina dropped the Huskies to 4-3 on the season.

Speaking to reporters after No. 7 UConn dropped its second game in the past three outings, Auriemma said, "I'm having a really hard time coaching this team. You might be able to tell that. I've got to figure it out. But it would be nice if I could get a little help."

The Huskies struggled mightily against the No. 1 team in the nation on Tuesday, shooting just 27 percent from the field and committing 18 turnovers.

Geno, Dawn Haven't Spoke Since Final Four 😬

Auriemma expressed his belief that his team has an ""unbelievably poor response to adversity all the time," and added, "It's just so out of character for anybody that's watched UConn play for 30-some years. I don't even recognize it."

UConn actually out-scored South Carolina in three out of four quarters on Tuesday, but a 27-6 second quarter in favor of the Gamecocks made all the difference.

The Huskies have now lost three games in the month of November, marking the first time that has happened in program history, per ESPN's Alexa Philippou .

While things have not been pretty for UConn thus far, it should be noted that Auriemma's team has played a remarkably difficult schedule during the early part of the season.

UConn's losses have come against the No. 1 team in the nation in South Carolina, as well as No. 2 Michigan and No. 3 Louisville, all of whom are undefeated.

Meanwhile, the Huskies did beat Iowa and Ohio State, who were Nos. 10 and 17 in the nation, respectively, at the time of the games.

UConn's schedule is not set to get any easier either, as three of the team's next four opponents are ranked.

It starts with No. 5 Duke on Saturday, followed by No. 18 Maryland on Dec. 5 and No. 13 Notre Dame on Dec. 9.

UConn won the national championship in 2025 and has reached the Final Four each of the past three seasons. It also has the reigning College Player of the Year in Sarah Strong on its roster.

All of those factors suggest the Huskies will eventually figure it out and get back in contention, but Auriemma's frustration is apparent as the team tries to find its way.

articles.title: NBA Cup 2026 Standings, Bracket Predictions After November 24 Group Play
articles.summary: The Dallas Mavericks and Detroit Pistons picked up critical wins in NBA Cup group play on Tuesday.
articles.body:
The Dallas Mavericks and Detroit Pistons picked up critical wins in NBA Cup group play on Tuesday.

Dallas took full control of West Group A with its road win over the Denver Nuggets.

The Mavericks are now in a win-and-in situation on Friday night in Phoenix.

The Pistons dropped the Orlando Magic to 3-1 in East Group A. That set up the potential for the Magic, Pistons and Toronto Raptors to all finish at 3-1 in East Group A.

A handful of massive games are ahead on Wednesday. The Miami Heat's trip to face the Philadelphia 76ers will go a long way in deciding East Group B, while the Minnesota Timberwolves and Oklahoma City Thunder square off for West Group B supremacy.

The Cade Cunningham-less Detroit Pistons altered the scenarios in Group A.

There's now a chance that the Pistons, Orlando Magic and Toronto Raptors all finish on 3-1 and the group title comes down to the point differential tiebreaker.

Orlando is done with its Group A games and it's at a bit of a disadvantage with its -1 point differential.

Detroit is at home to the Milwaukee Bucks on Friday, while Toronto welcomes the Brooklyn Nets north of the border.

The Pistons and Raptors are both incentivized to run up the score not just to jump Orlando, but to be in contention to advance as the best second-place team in the Eastern Conference.

The Atlanta Hawks, Cleveland Cavaliers and Philadelphia 76ers are the other competitors for the best second-place team spot going into Wednesday.

Atlanta is on the road at the Boston Celtics on Friday night. Boston's been the dominant team in East Group C with three wins and a +68 point differential.

Boston needs to beat Atlanta to secure first place in Group C. An Atlanta win would allow the Hawks to win Group C on the head-to-head tiebreaker.

Group B is still wide open. The Miami Heat visit Philadelphia and Cleveland visits the New York Knicks on Wednesday night.

Miami then goes to New York on Friday, while the Sixers finish up on the road with the Indiana Pacers.

A Miami win on Wednesday secures Group B for the Heat. At that point, the only team that could catch Miami is Cleveland, who the Heat beat two weeks ago.

A Sixers victory opens the door for them to control Group B. The Cavs are still in contention for first place as well.

The best second-place team will have one loss based on what's going on in Group A. The Knicks aren't eliminated yet, but it's looking more likely that they will be eliminated at the group stage.

The Dallas Mavericks' win on Tuesday night put them in excellent position to advance to the knockout round as the Group A winner.

The Mavs need to beat the Phoenix Suns on Friday to secure the top spot in Group A. They could also clinch first with a Phoenix loss to the Houston Rockets on Wednesday. That result would drop the Suns to 1-2 in group play with the inability to jump the Mavs on the head-to-head tiebreaker if they were to win on Friday.

Nikola Jokic and the Denver Nuggets need to run up the score on the Utah Jazz on Friday to have a shot at advancing as the best second-place team.

Denver is now rooting for the Minnesota Timberwolves to beat the Oklahoma City Thunder on Wednesday and for the San Antonio Spurs to defeat the Los Angeles Lakers on Friday.

In that scenario, Denver would be in a great spot to advance because its two top competitors would be taken out.

The Wolves can afford a road loss to the Thunder because they have another game to play at home on Friday night versus the Memphis Grizzlies.

Minnesota can clinch first place in Group B, though, with a win over OKC.

San Antonio needs to beat Portland on Wednesday and the Lakers on Friday to land first place in Group C.

Portland is fascinating because if it upsets the Spurs it could run the score up on the New Orleans Pelicans on Friday and be in a spot to advance.

Just like in the East, a second loss likely dooms a team from advancing because Denver and Minnesota, if it loses on Wednesday, isn't expected to lose more than one game.

articles.body: Cameron Brink, the 24 year old Los Angeles Sparks’ star player, has stepped into one of the happiest phases of her life as she has now tied the knot with her longtime partner, former Stanford rower Ben Felter on November 14, 2026, at Stanford University's Memorial Church in California. articles.title: 30 things to be thankful for in the NBA, including Victor Wembanyama's greatness and the Lakers' chemistry
articles.summary: As we approach the 20-game mark, let's dive into the things to be thankful for this season.
articles.body:
As we approach the 20-game mark in the NBA's regular season, I must say it's been a true joy to watch these teams compete — trying to learn what they're good at, where they struggle and adjusting on the fly. They may not have all the answers quite yet, but the effort is there. It can be easy to sit back and criticize, but ultimately it's more fulfilling to lead with gratitude. Here are 30 things I'm thankful for.

The month of November. Last year at this time, the Hawks went 10-5 with the ninth-best defensive rating in the league. So far this month they are 8-2 with the fifth-best defensive rating. Having a new level of wing depth thanks to the additions of Aaron Wiggins and Lu Dort has allowed them to balance different lineups through injuries. When the Hawks' defensive activity (see Daniels, Dyson) keeps opponents out of the paint, they get a chance to run and flow.

Their defense. Poor timing (like a recent four-game losing streak) can put a damper on things this time of year, but the Celtics have rarely had to worry about that on the defensive end of the floor. They have consistently defended as a unit, showing early help, swarming on any sort of dribble penetration and working to dictate terms on what types of shots they give up. This will be key as they navigate more and more teams working to trap Jayson Tatum on offense.

Thankfully, this is only the second time in 10 regular seasons that the Nets have started 3-13 (don't ask me how I know). Then again, this is now back-to-back seasons where they have started 3-13, with opponents scoring 129 or more points against them in five of their last seven games. If they can string together some stops, it may feel different. OK, on a brighter note, their broadcast team is elite and the ABA court is fire.

Who doesn't appreciate something that didn't look so fun on paper and then suddenly did? Look at the turnaround from the Bulls, who have found a balance offensively and some effort defensively. Buddy Hield has made 18 3s in his last four games! Nic Claxton is switching (again). Tiago Splitter is unafraid to expand his rotation and stick to what's working out there.

Sometimes reality, an honest conversation and a look in the mirror can be what you need. That's what the Hornets have received as their offense has plummeted and their defense has not held up to the pressure. Kon Knueppel has played only six minutes this season and the Hornets did start 4-12 last year before making a play-in run, so perhaps brighter days are ahead.

Sometimes the leftovers are better than the initial meal. Cleveland's record and consistency are likely not where it thought it would be after last year's deep run. But the moments where you see how much James Harden and Donovan Mitchell impact a game and how the Cavs' bench provides them a different type of energy means there could be a deeper payoff down the line.

Morez Johnson Jr.'s start. Sure, there is a consistency that Cooper Flagg is playing with and an ease that Kyrie Irving displays that sets up shots for everyone to contribute, but let's recognize the energy that Johnson brings to the table and the potential he has on the defensive end of the floor. Weakside communication and rotations should not be ignored, folks.

Their adaptability and understanding how to get the job done. The Nuggets have turned their season around by winning 9 out of 13 games and it feels like they are working to find ways to win different types of games — trusting a level of versatility whether it's an offensive shootout or their defense is getting stops. It also very much helps that Jamal Murray and Nikola Jokić are always at the table.

Their evolution continues to stand out. More movement, more flow, quicker decisions. They will have to find balance and avoid old habits, but continuing to move Ausar Thompson around the board before Jalen Duren returns is a good thing. Cade Cunningham, who sat out Tuesday with knee soreness, has continued to cook no matter who has been in the lineup.

It's Stephen Curry. The Warriors should be thankful they have Stephen Curry — who is averaging 27.8 points per game and shooting 45.7% from 3 at 38 years old — and hope he returns to the court as soon as possible.

The wisdom Fred VanVleet and Marcus Smart have delivered in spades. VanVleet, in particular, just has a way of making the exact play the Rockets need over and over again. He reads defenses to open things up, and makes them pay with shots when they anticipate the pass. Smart's ability to defend multiple positions puts everyone else in a more comfortable spot.

The uncompromising nature in which the Pacers play the game of basketball. No matter who is in the lineup, if shots are falling, if they are getting stops: they are going to work to play Pacers basketball. The ball is going to move, the drives are going to be there, the passes will persist. It might be Andrew Nembhard eating up space, Ivica Zubac making an impact in the paint or Pascal Siakam doing a little bit of everything. They don't stop. Just watch Kelly Oubre.

Brandon Ingram's return. Is there a chance that the talent on the Clippers can finally come together and maximize their ability to be bothersome in the Western Conference? Hope goes a long way, and the more scoring and playmaking the Clippers can have on the court the better. Darius Garland has been game, but the Clippers just need to sustain the good they find rather than reinvent the wheel.

The chemistry that has elevated the Lakers. Luka Dončić has been lights out, but the build around him has continued to pay off. They can get to multiple lineups and get consistent production up and down the roster. You never quite know who could help break a game open for them. Every night you can feel them attempting to accomplish the same goals on each end.

Internal growth. As tremendous as Ty Jerome and Cameron Boozer have been, has anyone been paying attention to the development from Cedric Coward and Cam Spencer? Coward hit 33.8% of his 3s last year and is shooting 44.7% from 3 this year while attempting more of them. Spencer continuously makes plays (and shots) within the flow of what the Grizzlies want to do. They are a team that believes in what they do every night and the internal growth shows it game in and game out.

Davion Mitchell, who has done everything this team has asked him to do and more. The defense speaks for itself, but the playmaking has grown. Mitchell is unafraid to direct the offense, he's reading defenses better, and his paint touches mean more. Mix in some shot-making and he's as happy as Klay Thompson running an empty-side action. Coach Spo has (once again) expanded his menu by mixing in pick-and-rolls or post-ups when needed, too.

Not all charcuterie boards are the same, but you can find the right combinations, even in the wildest ones. Brayden Burries' drives have been fun, but there is a rhythm that is helping him find consistency on the court. Him playing well while Tyler Herro gets all of the buckets is a positive sign. Herro scoring 50 and 32 in back-to-back games while shooting 60%+ from the field is not easy, either.

Consistency. It's not hard to see these Wolves play the game with a level of joy, but they also bring a level of steadiness, particularly on the defensive end. Rudy Gobert patrols the paint, but their ability to use their size and length to switch and bog teams down continues to ignite their transition attack. The fact that they can have this level of lineup consistency on both ends of the floor speaks to a different world in Minnesota.

The growth of Zion Williamson. It's been an up-and-down time in New Orleans, but that shouldn't take away from the Pelicans star's performance. The team has been more willing to switch him defensively and he's worked to hold up. The drives remain, but there's an ease to get to a short pull-up. He's even mixed in 3s on occasion. Tack on the consistent drives from Jeremiah Fears and there is still some potential on this plate.

Every single dish, dunk and drive from Karl-Anthony Towns this season. If last year was about KAT answering questions, this year has been about him delivering problems . The Knicks have been able to lean more into playing through him, opening their offense for everyone. He's also found the gaps to attack, making it tough on bigs and working to punish wings who switch. It also means you really don't know when and where Jalen Brunson is going to attack.

Trusting in your principles in the face of adversity. The Thunder know what they want to work toward and trust they can get there, but each night brings a different test as they navigate injuries. Lineups that used to be a strength (double big/small ball) may present new challenges with this group.

Franz Wagner playmaking. Sometimes you're asked to handle more responsibility or you graduate to a different table this time of year. Since Oct. 30, Wagner has six games where he has 10 or more assists. Prior to that he had done it only two times in his career. It's not just reading defenses, it's bending defenses and understanding what his move can do to force a defense to react. Positive sign for the Magic.

The ability to figure things out and adjust on the fly is always something to be thankful for. It's been a big reason why the Sixers have been able to climb to the top of the Eastern Conference. It may not be the ideal setting, but what in life is? Led by Tyrese Maxey, they are 12-0 in clutch games this season while shooting 50% from the field and 52% from 3 before they have everything figured out. That is a good sign.

Getting back to the basics. Success is not always linear, and just because you do something well once does not mean it will automatically transfer. Returning to the basics of what Phoenix likes to do defensively should help soften some of its offensive issues. It's always good to be self-aware in these moments. It helps that the Suns are 6-2 when Collin Gillespie scores 10 or more points.

Who doesn't love a good homecoming? The Damian Lillard return continues to pay off as the Blazers are able to get the most out of him without putting the total weight of the offense on him. And who doesn't love a good wing? Toumani Camara is a mad man, Sidy Cissoko has continued to defend multiple positions … and they are both making 3s?

It's the ground floor of the Darius Acuff Jr. Experience, and while the wins may not be there right now … sometimes you're in the building for something special before it truly becomes that. Whether it's the straight-line drives, the ability to get to his own shot when he wants or the reps to develop his playmaking, there is a payoff here.

Being able to watch Victor Wembanyama play basketball every single night. There is a moment in almost every game that feels like it's something you've never witnessed before. Criticism is fair, but greatness shouldn't be ignored.

Again, who doesn't appreciate a good wing? Toronto has them in bunches and they all deliver in different ways. The growing comfort of Scottie Barnes when it comes to getting to his shot in the midrange. Collin Murray-Boyles' ability to be everywhere at once on any given possession. Allen Graves and his quick hands; best of luck if you overpenetrate around him.

Opportunities for Darryn Peterson to grow. Injuries have taken their toll on this Jazz roster and the fact that 15 of their 19 games played have been against teams at .500 or above has not helped. But there have been plenty of chances for Peterson to develop as a playmaker and a defender. A lot of the issues feel controllable: the up-and-down ball movement, inconsistent defense and turnovers. You have to hope it gets better, but as Will Hardy said, hope is not a strategy.

Before Monday's loss to the Celtics, the Wizards had not just won three straight games, but had held three straight opponents to sub-100 points scoring. For the season, they have held opponents under 100 five times. They did it three times last year. Effort goes a long way.

articles.title: NBA Announces $11B Arena Initiative Amid Push for European League With FIBA
articles.summary: The NBA has announced an initiative to raise nearly $11 billion in funding to help renovate arenas in Europe as part of plans to launch the long-awaited continental league with FIBA.
articles.body:
The NBA has announced an initiative to raise nearly $11 billion in funding to help renovate arenas in Europe as part of plans to launch the long-awaited continental league with FIBA.

As reported by Tim Reynolds of the Associated Press, the NBA has revealed a robust group of investment firms that will support the renovation of stadiums across the region. This includes Apollo Sports Capital, Ares Management, Arctos, Blackstone, HPS Investment Partners and J.P. Morgan.

Back in October , both the NBA and FIBA confirmed a timeline that will see the division launched in 2027.

As noted in Reynolds' report, the league said the latest investment will provide "prospective clubs and ownership groups with access to sustainable capital and the NBA's expertise to develop modern arena facilities and, where appropriate, surrounding districts."

"We've seen firsthand how state-of-the-art arenas and the related developments around them can transform basketball teams and their surrounding communities," NBA Commissioner Adam Silver said, per Reynolds.

"As we prepare to launch a new league in Europe alongside FIBA, we see a significant opportunity to help clubs develop facilities which both build on the unique traditions that define European basketball while also elevating the fan experience and attracting many more live events."

EuroLeague owners previously rejected plans of a merger, with ESPN's Brian Windhorst reporting that they feel undervalued by NBA and FIBA. The two organizations continue to push forward with the conception of a new league, despite the resistance.

articles.title: Wemby's 'Moral High Horse' Reportedly Drawing Ire from NBA Players After Stat-Padding Comments
articles.summary: Players around the NBA have reportedly been judging San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama for sitting on what ESPN's Michael C. Wright described as a "moral high horse."
articles.body:
Players around the NBA have reportedly been judging San Antonio Spurs star Victor Wembanyama for sitting on what ESPN's Michael C. Wright described as a "moral high horse."

Wright discussed some players' perspective on Wembanyama on Wednesday's episode of Brian Windhorst & The Hoop Collective (1:29:30 mark of the video below).

"I've heard players around the league talking about Vic being like Mr. Morality, Mr. High Morals. 'Moral high horse' is what it's been described as," Wright said. "To hear him talk about— just admitting that he was stat-padding, that was refreshing."

Wemby 'Had to Show Off' for Selena Gomez

Wright's comment comes after Wembanyama spoke rather pointedly following a historic 50-point, 19-rebound stat line in a Saturday win over the New Orleans Pelicans.

"Unlike many of my peers, I'm not very good at stat-padding," Wembanyama said after the game about the third 50-ball of his career. "So I haven't reached it as many times as I should have."

The win over the Pelicans marked the second time this month Wembanyama hit the 50-point plateau after posing a career-high 52 points and 24 rebounds Nov. 4 against the Dallas Mavericks.

Those performances have helped Wembanyama average a personal-best 29.9 points per game through 17 contests this season. He was sidelined Monday by back tightness, but ESPN's Anthony Slater reported he is expected to return to the lineup Monday night against the Portland Trail Blazers.

articles.title: NBA anuncia al menos 10.000 millones de inversión en Europa con vista a su llegada en 2027
articles.standfirst: Sería "para el desarrollo y la renovación de pabellones de baloncesto, y los distritos deportivos y de entretenimiento que los rodean"
articles.summary: Sería "para el desarrollo y la renovación de pabellones de baloncesto, y los distritos deportivos y de entretenimiento que los rodean"
articles.body: La NBA, en su idea de poner en marcha "un nuevo ecosistema de baloncesto profesional en Europa en 2027" junto a la Federación Internacional de Baloncesto (FIBA), ha hecho oficial a través de un comunicado una iniciativa por la cual destinaría "al menos 10.000 millones de euros en financiación para el desarrollo y la renovación de pabellones de baloncesto, y los distritos deportivos y de entretenimiento que los rodean" en todo el continente. Para ello, la liga de baloncesto estadounidense contará con el respaldo de grandes grupos inversores entre los que se encuentran Apollo Sports Capital; Ares Management; Arctos, una división de KKR; Blackstone; HPS Investment Partners, parte de BlackRock; J.P. Morgan; Sixth Street o Stonepeak. De esta manera, todos ellos "buscarán asociarse con los clubes participantes, grupos propietarios, promotores locales y otros proveedores de servicios para desarrollar pabellones de primer nivel mundial que mejoren la experiencia del aficionado y, cuando corresponda, distritos de uso mixto alrededor de ellos", pudiendo incluir los proyectos "viviendas, espacios de trabajo, restaurantes, comercios y espacios públicos". "Hemos visto de primera mano cómo los pabellones de última generación y los desarrollos vinculados a su alrededor pueden transformar los equipos de baloncesto y las comunidades que los rodean. Mientras nos preparamos para lanzar una nueva liga en Europa junto con la FIBA, vemos una oportunidad significativa para ayudar a los clubes a desarrollar instalaciones que, por un lado, se apoyen en las tradiciones únicas que definen al baloncesto europeo y, por otro, eleven la experiencia del aficionado y atraigan muchos más eventos en directo", señala Adam Silver, comisionado de la NBA, en declaraciones incluidas en el texto. Por su parte, los inversores emitieron también un comunicado que aparece igualmente reflejado: "Estamos entusiasmados de trabajar con la NBA para apoyar una fase transformadora de desarrollo de infraestructuras en toda Europa. Juntos, tenemos el potencial de invertir miles de millones de euros para crear recintos de primer nivel mundial en ciudades europeas, honrando la pasión y las tradiciones de los aficionados al baloncesto europeo y respaldando un crecimiento económico duradero en las comunidades donde este deporte significa tanto".

articles.title: Markelle Fultz Reportedly Finds NBA Landing Spot After Not Signing Contract in Free Agency
articles.summary: After going unsigned as a free agent during the offseason, Markelle Fultz is returning to the Toronto Raptors organization.
articles.body:
After going unsigned as a free agent during the offseason, Markelle Fultz is returning to the Toronto Raptors organization.

Per HoopsHype's Michael Scotto , Fultz is joining the team's G League affiliate as a member of Raptors 905.

Fultz finished the 2025-26 season with the Raptors when he initially signed with their G League affiliate in March. He was given a 10-day contract by the NBA club two weeks later.

The Raptors used Fultz in five games at the end of March. He played a season-high 16 minutes in his first outing on March 23, a 143-127 win over the Utah Jazz.

Fultz played well during his time with Raptors 905. He averaged 11.0 points on 46.4 percent shooting, 5.9 assists and 2.4 rebounds per game in seven starts.

The G League season started on Nov. 6 with the tip-off tournament. Raptors 905 sport a 3-5 record thus far, but the roster has been hit hard by injuries. Nate Bittle, Andre Jackson Jr., Chucky Hepburn and Trey Jemison are all currently out of the lineup.

Blake Murphy of SportsNet noted Bittle and Jackson are getting close to returning.

Fultz, the No. 1 pick in the 2017 NBA draft, has appeared in 260 games over nine NBA seasons. The Washington alum has averaged 10.2 points, 4.3 assists and 3.1 rebounds per contest.

Fultz has had stints with the Raptors, Philadelphia 76ers, Orlando Magic and Sacramento Kings. He has appeared in a total of 26 NBA games since the start of the 2024-25 season.

articles.title: NBA Icon Chris Paul to Serve as 'College GameDay' Guest Picker Ahead of Wake Forest vs. Duke

NBA legend Chris Paul will return to his alma mater to serve as ESPN's College GameDay guest picker this weekend.

The former Demon Deacons star will appear on ESPN's broadcast ahead of the upcoming matchup featuring Duke at No. 8 Wake Forest, ESPN's Pat McAfee announced Wednesday.

Wake Forest climbed three spots in Tuesday's College Football Playoff rankings and will now look to secure a playoff berth by closing out the regular season with a win before facing No. 7 Miami in the ACC title game .
